title: Bandwidth-limited quantization throttling — microbench case notes
abstract: Short notes from a microbenchmark-driven investigation into cases where quantized kernels (INT8/AWQ/GPTQ and FP8 paths) hit a memory-bandwidth ceiling and cause throughput throttling despite low compute utilization. The aim: document methodology, evidence, and pragmatic mitigations we can try in the runtime.
body:
Background:
We repeatedly observed runs where token/sec flattened or even regressed after enabling INT8/AWQ kernels on certain model shapes (large decoder-only models, seq_len 1024, batch 1–4). GPU occupancy and SM utilization stayed below expected; wall-clock stalls correlated with high device memory traffic. Hypothesis: kernels optimized for compute produce more memory streaming (weights+KV traffic), causing device memory bandwidth to become the limiting factor.

Objectives:
1) Reproduce bandwidth-saturation behavior with minimal client variability (microbench harness).
2) Measure compute vs memory utilization across kernel variants (AWQ, GPTQ-packed, native FP8, FP32 baseline).
3) Identify kernel-level code patterns that exacerbate bandwidth (e.g., elementwise scatter, cache-unfriendly access patterns).
4) Propose runtime mitigations (prefetching, split compute, hybrid-quant fallback).

Environment and harness:
- Hardware: A100-SXM4-80GB and H100-80GB nodes (single GPU tests).
- CUDA 12.1, cuBLAS 12, driver 535.x.
- Telemetry collected: nv-nsight-cu-cli counters, nsys traces, nvml memory throughput estimates, /proc/gpu metrics, and our internal per-kernel counters (bytes read/write, DRAM traff metric approximation).
- Microbench harness: stripped-down generate loop with fixed prompt, warmup 30 steps, profile window 200 tokens at target sequence lengths. Token generation loop pinned to single host thread to reduce scheduling noise.
- Kernel set: AWQ-int8 (kernel-A), GPTQ-packed-int8 (kernel-B), FP8-optimized (kernel-C), FP32 baseline (kernel-Ref).

Test matrix (representative rows):
- Model shapes: 13B-decoder (emulated weights), 30B-decoder (subset), 70B-decoder (reduced layer count).
- Seq lengths: 128, 512, 1024
- Batch sizes: 1, 2, 4
- KV cache mode: streaming (no persistent pin), cache-keep (pinned pages)

Reproduction steps (short):
1) Build harness: tools/bench/quant_throttle_test --model X --kernel kernel-A --seqlen 1024 --batch 1 --warmup 30 --steps 200
2) Run nsys capture and nv-nsight counters in parallel to capture DRAM throughput and L2 hit rates.
3) Compare run with kernel-Ref (FP32) and kernel-B (GPTQ-packed) using same seed and prompt.

Key observations (raw):
- A100, 30B model, seqlen 1024, batch 1:
  - kernel-Ref (FP32): 18.3 tokens/sec, SM util 62%, estimated DRAM BW 540 GB/s (measured 56% of device rated).
  - kernel-A (AWQ-int8): 24.7 tokens/sec initially (first 50 tokens) then flattens to 14.1 tokens/sec; SM util 28%; DRAM BW measured ~78% of device rated during flat region.
  - kernel-B (GPTQ-packed): 22.9 tokens/sec steady; SM util 45%; DRAM BW ~65%.
  - kernel-C (FP8): 25.1 tokens/sec steady; SM util 58%; DRAM BW ~60%.
- H100 shows similar pattern but higher plateau throughput; AWQ still shows a post-warmup drop in many runs.

Interpretation notes:
- AWQ-int8 path shows an initial throughput bump then a sustained drop; the pattern aligns with warmup initially warming caches and then hitting repeated streaming patterns where DRAM requests dominate.
- SM utilization low during the flat/slow region indicates stalls waiting on memory rather than compute.
- GPTQ-packed performs better than AWQ in steady-state because its memory layout tends to allow better locality in the microbench shapes we used (packed blocks that align with vector loads), reducing total DRAM transfers.
- FP8 path is compute-favored and on these shapes does not expand memory footprint as aggressively, so it avoids hitting the same bandwidth ceiling.

Microcounter evidence (nsys summaries, representative):
- AWQ kernel (flat region): DRAM read throughput ~620 GB/s (device theoretical 900 GB/s), L2 miss rate 18%, global load throughput very high, memory write stalls visible in instruction timeline.
- GPTQ-packed: DRAM ~520 GB/s, L2 miss 12%, fewer global load bursts.

Hypothesized kernel contributors:
- Repeated unaligned loads during per-head dequant + scatter into KV buffers (AWQ path we use does an expand per token).
- No prefetch schedule in AWQ microkernel; dequant loops touch weight blocks repeatedly across heads causing re-streaming.
- GPTQ-packed kernel uses blockwise vector loads and better contiguous writes into KV buffer which reuses L2 more effectively.

Small code-level examples (pseudo):
- AWQ dequant loop fragment (simplified):
  for (i=0;i<n;i++) { out[i] = dequant(weight_ptr[i]); write_kv(out[i]); }
  -- causes many small, strided memory ops, poor L2 reuse.
- GPTQ packed fragment:
  for (i=0;i<n; i+=block) { v = vector_load(weight_ptr + i); deq = vector_deq(v); write_kv_block(deq); }
  -- larger contiguous transfers and more vector work on-chip.

Mitigations tried (and quick wins):
1) Kernel-level: change AWQ microkernel to block-loads (32–64 element blocks) + software prefetch of next block. Result: 12–18% steady-state throughput improvement in microbench, DRAM BW down by ~9%.
2) Runtime-level: dynamic kernel routing by seqlen/profiled token position. If predicted DRAM traffic > threshold, fallback to GPTQ-packed or FP8 for remainder of sequence. Result: avoids flat region but increases average latency for first tokens due to fallback overhead.
3) KV cache pinning (host pinned pages): reduced host-device transfer jitter but did not materially reduce device DRAM load (our issue is on-GPU DRAM).
4) Batch coalescing: grouping small concurrent requests to improve packing; effective when batch >1 but hurts p99 latency for single-user PLG flows.

Tradeoffs and risks:
- Block-load changes add code complexity and may increase register pressure, impacting parallelism for very small models.
- Runtime fallback policies add decisioning complexity and require accurate telemetry; misprediction can cause oscillation (flip-flopping between kernels).
- Prefetching helps but tuning is hardware-specific (H100 vs A100 prefetch distance differs).

Actionable recommendations (short):
- Short term (next 2 weeks): land a guarded block-load + prefetch variant of AWQ (A/B behind an env flag), run extended microbench sweep across model shapes and H100/A100 and collect delta telemetry. Open PR: github.com/redwood-inference/quant-kernels#87 (linked).
- Medium term (1–2 months): implement a profile-guided runtime routing rule: during warmup measure DRAM BW per-kernel for first N tokens and select steady-state kernel for remainder. Instrument with a simple hysteresis to avoid oscillation.
- Long term: re-evaluate AWQ packing strategy upstream; collaborate with research team to produce an AWQ packing variant that favors contiguous blocks aligned to vector lanes. Consider exposing a per-customer policy to prefer FP8 fallback for latency-sensitive single-user flows.

Notes and open questions:
- Why does AWQ dequant pattern differ so much across model shapes? Hypothesis: packing/quant layout chosen during quantization step (offline) interacts with kernel assumptions. Need to add a small reporter to quantization pipeline that records block stride and alignment per-layer.
- Can we cheaply estimate per-request DRAM pressure in our client-side profiler? Early experiments show a low-overhead running average of bytes read per inference correlates with the saturation point and can be used as a trigger.

Appendix: reproducible command examples:
- Run AWQ microbench with nsys capture:
  nsys profile --output awq-run --trace=cuda,nvtx --sample=none 
  ./tools/bench/quant_throttle_test --model 30B --kernel AWQ --seqlen 1024 --batch 1 --warmup 30 --steps 200

- Minimal perf counter capture (nsys) parsing: tools/telemetry/parse_nsys --input awq-run.qdrep --counters "dram_read_throughput, l2_miss_rate, sm_efficiency"

Owners/next steps: Daniel Chen (owner) to open PR for guarded kernel change; Aisha to run 48-hour microbench sweep; Marco to add a quantizer metadata emitter. Priya to scope runtime routing prototype.

results_summary:
Summary bullets:
- AWQ shows transient improvement then steady-state throttling tied to device DRAM BW.
- GPTQ-packed avoids worst case by improving memory locality.
- FP8 offers the most robust steady-state throughput on tested shapes.
- Block-load + prefetch yields measurable improvement and is a low-risk first change.
conclusions: Memory bandwidth is a first-class dimension in our quantization tradeoff space. Optimization efforts that focus only on compute (reduce FLOPs) can inadvertently increase DRAM transfers and hurt end-to-end throughput. Our runtime should be able to route away from bandwidth-heavy kernels when telemetry indicates pressure.
